stories.headline: Update: Trump Arrives in China for Three-Way Talks With Xi and Putin
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump arrived in China on Wednesday for the APEC summit in Shenzhen, where he is set to hold the first-ever three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday. Xi personally greeted Trump on arrival, offering a hug and a red-carpet welcome in what coverage described as a rare and surprising gesture. Crowds gathered in Shenzhen to welcome the U.S. president.

Trump came from the Philippines, where he attended the ASEAN summit, met regional partners and sought to formalize a trade deal. The trip offers a break from setbacks at home, including a major disruption to U.S. aviation and the espionage scandal that brought down Nvidia chief Jensen Huang. Reports said Trump avoided discussing the Huang case with Xi.

The talks are expected to address the war involving Iran, the war in Ukraine and trade. Trump is also expected to hold a one-on-one meeting with Putin, following White House efforts to broker an end to the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Washington has criticized Kyiv for not signing deals that Ukraine believes would cede too much territory, while European leaders have accused Moscow of stalling negotiations.

The summit unfolds against active U.S.-Iran hostilities and heightened tensions among major powers. Supporters of the president's approach say direct engagement with rival leaders is the surest route to ending conflicts, while critics worry about concessions to Moscow and Beijing. Outcomes of Thursday's meetings are expected to shape the trajectory of both the Ukraine and Iran conflicts.

stories.headline: Anthropic Prices IPO at $83 a Share, Valuing Company Above $1 Trillion
stories.summary:
Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI models, priced its initial public offering at $83 per share, Axios confirmed, giving the company an initial market capitalization of about $1.08 trillion and a fully diluted value near $1.5 trillion. The price came in well above the planned range of $70 to $78 per share. Shares are set to begin trading on Nasdaq on Thursday.

The offering is one of the largest IPOs in history. The company could raise significantly more if underwriters exercise their so-called greenshoe option to purchase additional shares. Anthropic will become by far the largest publicly traded public benefit corporation, a structure that requires it to balance safety with profit.

The listing is expected to place Anthropic among the ten most valuable U.S. companies. It arrives amid recent turmoil in the AI sector, including the espionage case that led to the departure of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and a series of technology outages. Wall Street's appetite for the offering suggests investors still expect the AI boom to continue.

The company also faces scrutiny, including a lawsuit from California's attorney general over alleged safety failures. Its first day of trading will be watched as a barometer of investor confidence in the broader AI industry.

stories.headline: Update: House Democrats Nominate Jeffries for Speaker in 251-11 Vote
stories.summary:
House Democrats voted at a closed-door caucus meeting Wednesday to nominate Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York as their candidate for speaker. Jeffries won 251 of 262 votes cast, well above the 218 needed on the House floor. The vote was tallied at Jeffries' request, after skeptics had pushed for a recorded count.

The result positions Jeffries to become the first Black speaker in U.S. history when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, after Democrats take control of the House. Some members were not unanimous in their support, and activists have urged lawmakers to block him, but most colleagues said they expected him to win and wanted the matter settled.

Jeffries is expected to be one of President Trump's most prominent opponents during the final two years of his term. Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming Oversight Committee chair, began laying groundwork for investigations, sending document-retention letters to Vice President Vance, Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump and Jared Kushner, among others. Republicans have criticized the planned probes as partisan, while Democrats say they are exercising oversight.

Separately, House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie, a Republican, asked interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to appear before his panel as scrutiny of the Nvidia espionage case grows.

stories.headline: Voyager 1 Becomes First Human-Made Object One Light-Day From Earth
stories.summary:
NASA's Voyager 1 on Wednesday became the first human-made object to travel one light-day, about 16 billion miles, from Earth. Launched in 1977, the probe is traveling faster than 37,000 mph through interstellar space at the far reaches of the solar system. For perspective, NASA's Jason Rhodes noted the sun is only about eight light-minutes from Earth.

At this distance, a radio signal takes a full day to reach the spacecraft and another day for a reply to return. NASA communicates with Voyager through the Deep Space Network of giant antennas in California, Spain and Australia. Rhodes called it a testament to the engineering of a craft launched nearly 50 years ago.

Voyager 1 and its twin Voyager 2 were sent to explore the giant outer planets, using a rare planetary alignment for gravity assists. Voyager 1 left the planets behind after Saturn in 1980, and in 1990 took the "Pale Blue Dot" photograph of Earth before its cameras were turned off. It continues to send data from interstellar space.

stories.headline: Fed's Waller Says Officials May Need to 'Shock' Markets With Half-Point Rate Hike
stories.summary:
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said Wednesday that central bank officials may need to "shock people" at their next policy meeting in early December, signaling he may back a half-point interest rate increase. In an interview with CNBC's Steve Liesman, Waller said he is "very concerned" about inflation.

Waller said a "vast majority" of officials worry that inflation could prove persistent even if gasoline prices continue to decline. He pointed to the lingering effects of tariffs and the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure as factors that could keep price pressures elevated, even if those influences eventually fade.

A half-point increase would be a larger move than the quarter-point steps the Fed typically favors, and Waller's remarks serve as a signal to markets ahead of the December meeting. Rate decisions affect borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans, credit cards and business lending across the economy. The comments come as the Fed already faces political pressure and internal debate, and investors will watch for whether other governors echo his stance before the meeting.

stories.headline: Israeli Military Launches Rare Ground Operation in Gaza Beyond Yellow Line
stories.summary:
Israeli ground forces launched a rare operation Wednesday in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents. Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the main north-south road under cover of artillery strikes.

The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation, conducted jointly with the Shin Bet security service, aims to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the boundary of the more than 60 percent of Gaza that Israel occupies. It said the tunnel posed an immediate threat to troops and that forces are operating in accordance with the ceasefire agreement. A section of Salah al-Din road was closed to traffic.

Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, called the advance a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire and "a dangerous development." Residents described gunfire and shelling, and one said there were numerous casualties, including fatalities; the Israeli military offered only a general statement when asked. Violence has continued through the 13 months of the ceasefire, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and conditions for Gaza's 2.1 million people remain dire.

stories.headline: Hegseth Makes Unannounced Trip to Caracas, Signs Military Agreement With Venezuela
stories.summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made an unannounced trip to Caracas on Wednesday and met Venezuelan acting President Delcy Rodríguez. He signed a military agreement with Venezuela and announced the United States will deepen its defense partnership with the country.

Hegseth said the cooperation would help counter foreign actors and "narco-terrorists," and that U.S. forces would help Venezuela's military combat drug cartels. He said Washington looks forward to "following through, deepening our defense cooperation and our defense partnership."

The visit marks a significant shift in the relationship between the two governments. Details of the agreement, including the scope of any U.S. military presence or operations, were not immediately available. The move follows reports of a U.S. troop buildup elsewhere in the region, and it is likely to draw scrutiny in Congress and across Latin America over its terms and implications.

stories.headline: Senate Advances Bipartisan Permitting Reform Bill 65-31
stories.summary:
The Senate took a series of key votes Wednesday advancing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a permitting reform bill meant to speed the nation's ability to build infrastructure and energy projects. The chamber advanced the measure 65-31, clearing the Senate's 60-vote threshold and moving it toward final passage.

Supporters of the bill say faster permitting would cut delays and costs for projects ranging from pipelines and transmission lines to clean energy facilities. Speeding up permits for clean energy could also help fight global warming, a point emphasized by proponents of the legislation.

Many environmentalists, however, fear that other provisions in the bill go too far and could weaken environmental review. The lopsided bipartisan margin suggests broad support in the chamber, though the final shape of the bill and its fate in the House remain to be determined.

stories.headline: Grand Theft Auto 6 Earns Near-Perfect Critic Scores Ahead of Release
stories.summary:
The first reviews of Grand Theft Auto 6 are in, and critics have responded with almost uniform praise. Review aggregator Metacritic averages the game at 99 out of 100, tying The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998. The title arrives after a 13-year wait, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays.

IGN called the game "unprecedented" and "unmissable," while Eurogamer gave it five stars and said developer Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again." Bloomberg's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in a five-star review, and The Washington Post said it "raises the bar at every level." The Guardian praised the lifelike depiction of Leonida, the Miami-inspired setting, and the relationship between lead characters Jason and Lucia.

Some reviewers raised reservations. Eurogamer noted "there are also nits to pick," and The New York Times wondered whether the game's realism and the consequences attached to every action might dull the chaotic fun of earlier entries. Some online forum posters have objected to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype."

Rockstar has not disclosed the cost of the game, though some estimates put development spending above $1 billion. The title is widely regarded as one of the most anticipated releases in entertainment history, and its commercial performance will be closely watched by the games industry.

stories.headline: Haiti's Gang Violence Blocks Aid as Child Malnutrition Worsens
stories.summary:
More than a quarter of a million young Haitian children will suffer from acute malnutrition by next year, according to an international report released Tuesday. The report warns that mass displacement driven by gang violence is deepening what it describes as a devastating humanitarian crisis. Gang control of key roads and areas is blocking the delivery of food and medical assistance.

Separately, Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele said his forces destroyed another stronghold belonging to a Haitian gang leader. His forceful use of military power has electrified parts of the troubled Caribbean nation, even as it worries critics who fear abuses and the long-term consequences of such tactics.

The findings highlight the humanitarian cost of Haiti's prolonged security collapse, in which armed groups have displaced large numbers of people and disrupted basic services. Aid agencies continue to struggle to reach affected communities while violence persists.

stories.headline: Inside the Old Gas Pipeline Where Ukraine Is Fighting an Underground War With Russia
stories.summary:
For the past seven months, Ukrainian forces have lived and fought Russian troops inside an old Soviet gas pipeline in the Kharkiv region. The BBC is the first international broadcaster to enter the pipeline, where the subterranean battle is taking place near Kupyansk.

With a diameter of just over a metre, the pipeline leaves room only to crawl. It is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line, which have made it nearly impossible for either side to advance on the surface.

The BBC's defence correspondent Jonathan Beale went underground with the 13th Khartiia Operational Brigade. The report illustrates how drone warfare is pushing soldiers into unconventional positions and contributing to a grinding stalemate along the front.

stories.headline: British Scattered Spider Hacker Sentenced to Six Years in US Prison for $11.6 Million Theft
stories.summary:
Tyler Buchanan, a 24-year-old British hacker from Dundee, was sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the United States. He conspired to hack at least a dozen companies through text message phishing and stole more than $11.6 million in cryptocurrency from individual victims. Buchanan was part of the young hacker collective known as Scattered Spider, which has been blamed for a string of high-profile cybercrimes.

Prosecutors said the group sent hundreds of SMS messages to employees of large technology and telecommunications firms, directing them to spoof websites that harvested credentials. The stolen information was then used with SIM-swapping techniques to target cryptocurrency investors. The largest single theft was $1.67 million in December 2022, and prosecutors said the thefts had "severe, life-altering consequences" for victims.

The sentence concludes a years-long international investigation involving authorities in the UK, US, Spain and Canada. Buchanan began the campaign in 2021 at age 19, working from his parents' home. He was also a victim of rival hackers, who leaked his identity and address in 2023, and researchers say he was assaulted at his home.

stories.headline: Fed Governor Lisa Cook Declines to Appear Before White House Committee Weighing Her Removal
stories.summary:
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook has declined, through her lawyers, to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired. In a letter released Tuesday to White House counsel William Scharf, her attorney Abbe David Lowell called the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome.

Lowell wrote that Cook "has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing," and that she has "a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution's unique status and independence." The refusal sets up a direct confrontation over whether a president can remove a sitting Fed governor and under what process.

The dispute arrives as Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, whose four-year term began on May 22, is overhauling the central bank. He has shelved forward-looking guidance and changed the schedule of Federal Open Market Committee rate-setting meetings. Supporters of the administration argue the president has authority to hold officials accountable and that the review is a legitimate inquiry. Cook's defenders and many economists counter that a for-cause removal conducted this way threatens the political independence that underpins the Fed's credibility with markets.

The committee is expected to proceed with its review next month with or without Cook's participation. Any decision to remove her would likely trigger immediate legal challenges and close attention from financial markets.

stories.headline: Update: Iran Attacks Kuwait and Bahrain After US Strikes Qeshm Island Missile Site
stories.summary:
Kuwait and Bahrain said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise. The drone attack on Kuwait was the first in more than two months. Iran's army said it targeted Ali Al Salem Air Base, which hosts US forces, including Patriot air defense systems and launch platforms. Kuwaiti authorities reported no damage or casualties.

The attacks followed US warplanes striking an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz with precision munitions, according to US military officials. Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, said it intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks and has reported four attacks in six days after a two-month lull. Separately, the UAE's state oil firm said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf on Tuesday.

Kuwait's foreign ministry said the attack flagrantly violated its sovereignty and international law. Qatar, which has mediated stalled indirect talks between Washington and Tehran, called the strikes a dangerous escalation that threatens efforts to contain tensions. Iranian army commander Maj Gen Amir Hatami warned that any new attack would be met with a stronger response "without geographic limitations."

The nine-month-old war began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February. Deadlocked peace negotiations and the renewed exchanges have raised fears of a wider escalation affecting Gulf states and global oil and gas shipments through Hormuz.

stories.headline: Waymo Suspends Driverless Freeway Service Across All US Markets
stories.summary:
Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways. The decision follows California's ban on the company's driverless taxis on state freeways, which took effect on November 11 after a series of traffic incidents.

California's Department of Motor Vehicles cited an "imminent hazard to public safety," pointing to recurring incursions by Waymo vehicles into active construction zones where workers and equipment are present. One incident this month involved several driverless Waymo vehicles entering a construction zone on US Route 101 south of San Francisco. Waymo said no injuries or collisions were reported. Separate footage that spread on social media appeared to show a Waymo car trying to overtake patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing traffic on a San Francisco highway.

The California restriction will stay in place until Waymo demonstrates that it has taken effective corrective actions. A Waymo spokesperson said the company restricted freeway operations in its other markets to evaluate its performance and is working with state officials to resume service. The company says its data shows 95 percent fewer serious-injury crashes than human drivers.

Waymo operates in 15 US cities but offered freeway rides in only a handful, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami. Service on regular city streets continues. The move adds to regulatory scrutiny of the company, which recalled thousands of vehicles in May over a software issue involving flooded roads.

stories.headline: Biden Releases Memoir 'Promise Me, America' Detailing Presidency and Decision to Exit 2024 Race
stories.summary:
Former President Joe Biden's memoir, "Promise Me, America," was released Wednesday, nearly two years after he left office. The book recounts his time in the White House, including the pandemic response, the aftermath of the January 6 attack, the American Rescue Plan, the Infrastructure Act, the CHIPS Act and rallying NATO after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Biden is not conducting a traditional book tour. His former counselor Steve Ricchetti said the former president has a stage 4 cancer diagnosis, disclosed last May, that has spread to his bones, requires heavy medication and affects his energy. Ricchetti and other former aides are sharing the media load on his behalf.

Much of the attention centers on his decision to run for re-election in 2024 and later drop out. Ricchetti said Biden waited until after the midterms so the book would not become part of the campaign debate. Those midterms were widely seen as a referendum on President Trump's first two years of his second term, and Democrats won control of Congress.

The book arrives as Democrats reassess their direction and as critics, including some in his own party, continue to question whether Biden should have sought a second term given concerns about his age. Supporters point to his legislative record, while Republicans have long argued his presidency was marked by decline and policy failures.

stories.headline: Update: Rubio Says US Not 'Under Systemic Attack' After Series of Tech Outages
stories.summary:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday there is "zero evidence" linking the string of technology outages that have hit the United States over the past week. "We are not under systemic attack," he told reporters, adding that the events "are not inter-related." He acknowledged that "people are fearful" that the disruptions could be part of a coordinated plot.

Rubio's remarks came hours after Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Fox News the outages were not the product of a cyber-attack, and that "lots of institutions" are patching or upgrading systems, which has caused some disruption. Rubio said the best way to counter public fears, including the possibility of stockpiling or a run on banks, is for the government to share everything it knows. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin separately dismissed the idea of a coordinated attack and suggested artificial intelligence-driven code changes could be a factor, a claim that was described as far from conclusive.

The disruptions began last Thursday with a large Microsoft outage affecting email and other services. On Friday the FAA ordered a national ground stop lasting more than four hours, the longest halt to US flights since the September 11, 2001 attacks. On Monday a United Airlines technology failure delayed about 150 flights and a JPMorgan Chase software problem disrupted service at major banks.

On Tuesday, Apple's iCloud and Apple Pay suffered an outage the company attributed to an internal update, and a classified NSA internal network went offline for a time. Every affected company or agency has said the problem was not cyber-related or the work of an outside actor, and cybersecurity experts say there is no evidence connecting the incidents, though many cite aging infrastructure and rushed updates as common themes.

stories.headline: Trump Says US Expanding Defense Cooperation With Philippines, Cites Trade Deal
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump told Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Wednesday that Washington is expanding defense cooperation with its treaty ally. He said the two countries could also work together on a major civilian nuclear energy project.

Trump also said he has signed a "very big trade deal" with the Philippines but offered no details of the agreement. He described it as having come together quickly and called it "a magnificent deal for both" countries, adding that officials were pleased with it and had not expected it to happen so fast.

The Philippines is a longtime US treaty ally and a key partner in the Indo-Pacific. The announcement comes as Trump is engaged in diplomacy across the region, and further specifics on the defense and nuclear proposals have yet to be released.

stories.headline: Update: Asia Stocks Cling to Gains After Nvidia Earnings Beat, Anthropic Pricing Looms
stories.summary:
Stocks in Asia edged higher Wednesday after Nvidia reported better-than-expected results and a stronger sales forecast, even as uncertainty persists over the company's leadership. Oil prices fell after data showed rising US inventories.

Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion and net income of $65.3 billion, both more than double the year-earlier figures. It was the company's first earnings report since Jensen Huang was ousted as CEO in a scandal that has reportedly led to an SEC investigation.

Huang said earlier Tuesday that he would return to lead the chipmaker if the board invited him. Investors remain anxious for guidance on Nvidia's strategic roadmap, given its central role in the AI economy. Markets are also awaiting the pricing of an Anthropic offering.

stories.headline: Philippine Police Ask Prosecutors to Charge Thomas Markle Over Child Sex Abuse Material
stories.summary:
Police in the Philippines have asked prosecutors to charge Thomas Markle Sr., father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, with possession and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material. Cebu province prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC that police filed the request Monday, seeking two counts of intent to distribute and one count of possession.

Earlier this month Markle, 82, was separately arrested and charged in the United States with possession of such material. The FBI said agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books, from storage units he rented. He was returned to custody last week after prosecutors alleged he removed an ankle monitor while held at his Florida assisted living facility.

Philippine police obtained a warrant last month to examine devices allegedly removed from his former home there, which Thomas Markle Jr. handed over. Markle has denied the allegations. Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018 and said she was deeply distressed and that her thoughts were with any children who may have been harmed.
